nodes.name: Ru Nanoparticles Electrodeposition
nodes.procedure: Electrochemical deposition of Ru nanoparticles (ca. 10.6 μg cm⁻²) on RANEYs Ni conducted by performing cyclic voltammetry with RANEYs Ni as working electrode and electrolyte consisting of 0.5 M H₂SO₄ with (NH₄)₂RuCl₆. When negative voltage applied to RANEYs Ni, Ru cations adsorbed and deposited on surface, coinciding with electrolyte color transition from yellow to transparent. Ru precursor concentration and pH optimized to reduce mass loading from 47.4 to 10.6 μg cm⁻² while preserving HER performance.

unit_operations.name: Cyclic Voltammetry Electrodeposition
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: performing cyclic voltammetry with RANEYs Ni as a working electrode and an electrolyte consisting of 0.5 M H₂SO₄ with (NH₄)₂RuCl₆. When a negative voltage is applied to RANEYs Ni, Ru cations are adsorbed and then deposited on the surface of RANEYs Ni

unit_operations.name: Optimization
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: To optimize Ru_NPs electrodeposition, we adjusted both the Ru precursor concentration and pH, reducing the mass loading from 47.4 to 10.6 μg cm⁻² while preserving the HER performance

nodes.source_text: As shown in Fig. 2a, the electrochemical deposition of Ru_NPs was conducted by performing cyclic voltammetry... To optimize Ru_NPs electrodeposition, we adjusted both the Ru precursor concentration and pH...

nodes.description: HER performance in 1.0 M KOH three-electrode system
nodes.source_text: We firstly evaluated the HER performance of ${ \bf { R u } }_{ \mathrm { { N P s } } } @ { \bf { R A N E Y } }^{ \mathrm { \ @ } } Ni in 1.0 M KOH at $2 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in a three-electrode system. Commercial $\mathrm { P t / C }$ and blank RANEYs Ni were selected as benchmarks. The iR-corrected polarization curves show that the overpotential of ${ \bf { R u } }_{ \mathrm { { N P s } } } @ { \bf { R A N E Y } }^{ \mathrm { \ @ } } Ni is only $6 2 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ at a current density of $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m A } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , much lower than those of commercial $\mathrm { P t / C }$ $( 1 9 0 \ m V )$ and RANEYs Ni $( 1 8 0 ~ \mathrm { m V } )$. Furthermore, ${ \bf { R u } }_{ \mathrm { { N P s } } } @ { \bf { R A N E Y } }^{ \mathrm { \ @ } } Ni maintains the lowest Tafel slope value of $3 2 \mathrm { ~ m V ~ d e c } ^ { - 1 }$ compared to those of Pt/C $( 6 0 \mathrm { m V \ d e c ^ { - 1 } } )$ and RANEYs Ni $( 7 8 ~ \mathrm { m V d e c ^ { - 1 } } )$.

nodes.description: AWE electrolyzer performance with SSM anode at 80°C, 30 wt% KOH
nodes.source_text: As shown in Fig. 3c, the $\mathbf { R u } _ { \mathbf { N P s } } @ \mathbf { R A }-$ NEYs Ni||SSM electrolyzer demonstrated superior water splitting performance, which required lower voltages of $1 . 6 5 ~ \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and 1.74 V to achieve current densities of 0.5 A $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and $1 . 0 \mathrm { A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , respectively... current density of our electrolyzer reached as high as $1 0 \mathrm { A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ at a low cell voltage of $2 . 3 \mathrm { V }$... exhibited excellent stability, operating for 2500 hours at a current density of $1 . 0 \mathrm { A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$... low voltage decay of less than $4 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { V } ~ \mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$... low energy consumption of 3.95 and 4.20 kWh... faradaic efficiency of $9 8 . 6 \%$.

nodes.description: Large-scale AWE performance for 100 cm² electrode at 80°C
nodes.source_text: We further tested a $\mathrm { R u } _ { \mathrm { N P s } } @ \mathrm { R A N E Y ^ { \mathrm { \scriptscriptstyle G } } \ N i } \| \mathrm { S S M }$ based AWE electrolyzer with an electrode area of $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } } ^ { 2 }$ in $3 0 \mathrm { w t \% }$ KOH solution. The tested AWE electrolyzer exhibited a record high current of 100 A at a low cell voltage of 1.8 V... At $1 . 0 \mathrm { A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , the cell voltage of the $1 . 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ AWE electrolyzer was approximately $1 . 7 4 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$... which was slightly lower than that of the $1 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ AWE electrolyzer (1.80 V). In addition, the $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ production increased from 18.3 to 41.2 NL $\mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$... energy consumption decreased from 4.60 to 4.20 kWh... energy efficiency of $\mathbf { R u } _ { \mathrm { N P s } } @ \mathbf { R A N E Y } ^ { \mathrm { ( B ) } }$ Ni was calculated to be $8 4 . 2 \%$ (based on the higher heating value of hydrogen) and the price of the produced $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ was calculated to be $0 . 9 3 ~ \ S ~ \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$

nodes.evidence_snippet: The energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) elemental mapping images, coupled with SEM images (Fig. 2c and Fig. S7) show a uniform distribution of Ru and Ni elements.

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM shows lattice spacings of 0.23 nm and 0.21 nm, corresponding to Ru (111) and Ni (111) planes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 2d presents a high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image of RuNPs@RANEY® Ni, showing lattice spacings of 0.23 nm and 0.21 nm, corresponding to the lattice spacings of Ru (111) and Ni (111) planes, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Normalized Ru K-edge XANES spectra show K-edge absorption intensity and edge energy of Ru closely align with Ru foil.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 2e, K-edge absorption intensity and edge energy of Ru in RuNPs@RANEY® Ni closely align with those of Ru foil.

nodes.characterization_summary: Fourier transforms show predominant peak at 2.67 Å for Ru–Ru bonds; coordination number of Ru–Ru bonds is approximately 9.7.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Fourier transforms of EXAFS (Fig. 2f) show a predominant peak around 2.67 Å for Ru–Ru bonds... the EXAFS fitting curve... suggests that the coordination numbers of Ru–Ru bonds are approximately 9.7.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman shows broad O–H stretching bands from 2800-3800 cm^-1 deconvoluted into 4-HB·H2O (~3250 cm^-1), 2-HB·H2O (~3450 cm^-1), and K·H2O (~3600 cm^-1); K·H2O proportion increases to 16.8% at cathodic potentials.
nodes.evidence_snippet: All Raman spectra exhibited broad bands at wavenumbers from 2800 to 3800 cm^-1... Gaussian fitting... results in three distinct regions... K·H2O proportion for RuNPs@RANEY® Ni increased from 0 to 16.8%.

visual_evidence.name: In situ Raman spectra at -30 mV

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS shows RuNPs@RANEY® Ni retains surface metallic Ni state post-stability testing, unlike bare RANEYs Ni which oxidizes to Ni^2+/Ni^3+.
nodes.evidence_snippet: XPS analysis revealed RuNPs@RANEY® Ni retains its surface metallic Ni state post-stability testing, whereas bare RANEYs Ni undergoes complete oxidation to Ni^2+/Ni^3+ species.

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS reveals charge transfer resistance (R_ct) of 0.21 Ω, lower than Pt/C (1.43 Ω) and RANEYs Ni (1.65 Ω).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) reveals lower charge transfer resistance (0.21 Ω) than those of Pt/C (1.43 Ω) and RANEYs Ni (1.65 Ω) (Fig. S14).

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD pattern shows Ni (111), (200), and (220) planes at 44.5°, 51.8°, and 76.3° respectively; no metallic Ru detected due to low content.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The XRD pattern of RuNPs@RANEYs Ni shows Ni (111), (200), and (220) planes at 44.5°, 51.8°, and 76.3° (Fig. S10), respectively, and no metallic Ru is detected due to its low content.

nodes.characterization_summary: SAED confirms presence of Ru (111) planes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) results (Fig. S8) confirm the presence of Ru (111) planes.
